entries.title: Germany news: DB hampered by 'organized irresponsibility'
entries.summary: DB chief Evelyn Palla wants to move away from the culture of ''organized irresponsibility" by empowering new decision-makers within the railway operator. Brass musicians in Bavaria hope to set a new record. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: DB hampered by 'organized irresponsibility'

Published August 1, 2026last updated August 2, 2026

DB chief Evelyn Palla wants to move away from the culture of ''organized irresponsibility" by empowering new decision-makers within the railway operator. Brass musicians in Bavaria hope to set a new record. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • DB's Evelyn Palla sets 2035 as goal for completing major reforms within railway company
  • Pride events are taking place in several German cities a week after a deadly attack on a Pride march in Berlin
  • Authorities warn of holiday traffic disruption in Germany amid the two-hour closure of a key pass road in Austria
  • A forest fire is burning out of control in the Upper Palatinate region of Bavaria, with four firefighters so far injured in the blaze

Here is a round-up of some of the main stories from and about Germany hitting the headlines on the weekend of August 1-2.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Deutsche Bahn chief Evelyn Palla blasts 'organized irresponsibility' in the company

Deutsche Bahn chief Evelyn Palla blasts 'organized irresponsibility' in the company

The culture inside Germany's Deutsche Bahn (DB) is already shifting but the current crisis will take years to overcome, the head of the national railway company told Germany's Welt am Sonntag.

CEO Evelyn Palla criticized the old decision-making process in DB, saying that the central management often made big decisions on the operative level.

"The people in the headquarters, who made those decisions, don't have any responsibility for implementing them in the field," Palla said. "They have to be implemented by colleagues who are out there. But they say 'I didn't make this call, and it also doesn't work for me.' Then the headquarters says 'I have no operational responsibility, those people in the field did not implement [the decision] properly.' In the end it was something like organized irresponsibility."

She told the paper that much has been "reformed" and "slimmed down" since she took the reins of the state-owned firm last October, and that multiple administration levels inside DB had been cut.

"But all of that does not make for a better (Deutsche) Bahn," she added. "Things will only change when the management changes, when decentralized units take responsibility and live with it."

In the interview published on Sunday, she also said that the German railway network was "run into the ground by 25 years of saving money" and that tangible improvements will take time.

She pointed to DB's 200-year anniversary coming in 2035, saying that "this should be the year when the worst is behind us."

Skip next section We are resuming our coverage

We are resuming our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage of top news stories from Germany on this early August weekend.

On Sunday, Berlin is preparing for an anti-Islamist march in response to the deadly terror attack which shook Germany to the core a week ago.

In Bavaria, some 1,800 brass musicians are hoping to break the record for the world's longest concert as they near the end of the unprecedented 72-hour live performance.

And Evelyn Palla, the head of Germany Deutsche Bahn, is decrying "organized irresponsibility" inside the troubled railway company.

We will be bringing you more on these and other stories from Germany in this live blog.

Skip next section We've paused coverage

We've paused coverage

Thank you for reading the weekend edition of our blog about Germany and be sure to check in on Sunday morning to stay up to date with the latest headlines out of the country.

Skip next section WATCH — Hamburg Pride draws 300,000 after Berlin terror attack

WATCH — Hamburg Pride draws 300,000 after Berlin terror attack

Hamburg's Pride parade went ahead under heightened security, one week after a 21-year-old drove a van into crowds at Berlin Pride. The attack killed one person and injured 29 others.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

IN DEPTH: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. 

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests: 260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

Read more about Germany's policy on deportations to Afghanistan.

Skip next section Klingbeil urges for solidarity with Spain over Ceuta border breach

Klingbeil urges for solidarity with Spain over Ceuta border breach

German Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil on Saturday called on Europeans to stand by Spain amid the debate over the surge of migrants into Ceuta.

Footage showing tens of thousands of migrants crossing into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta raised concerns across the European Union.

"Migrants were used in an attempt to divide Europe," Klingbeil said.

He noted that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had restored control quickly and that most migrants who entered Ceuta had already returned to Morocco.

"Especially in situations like these, Europe must not allow itself to be divided," Klingbeil said.

Klingbeil's comments come after Italy officially suspended the Schengen agreement with Spain for one month in response to the mass crossing in Ceuta.

Skip next section Popular German national park closed after storm leaves 1 dead

Popular German national park closed after storm leaves 1 dead

A popular park in eastern Germany was closed to visitors on Saturday after a storm caused damage and left one person dead overnight.

A 38-year-old man was killed on Friday evening near the Felsenbühne open-air theater in Rathen when he was struck by a falling tree.

Ten other people were injured, three of them seriously, while 40 people were evacuated.

Emergency crews resumed clean-up operations on Saturday.

Authorities closed the area between the Bastei rock formation, the villages of Rathen and Hohnstein, and the Polenztal valley, citing ongoing safety risks for visitors.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany weighs the future of minijobs

IN DEPTH: Germany weighs the future of minijobs

When Anahita Abdollahi starts her shift, she first checks her emails to make sure she's up to date on all the library requests.

The 26-year-old master's student from Iran describes her job as a "part-time librarian" — she helps people find books they need for their studies, answers phone calls, and waters the plants.

This type of employment is known in Germany as a "minijob," a system that allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions.

Skip next section WATCH: German development aid: Is soft power in decline?

WATCH: German development aid: Is soft power in decline?

German funding for projects abroad is falling. So is public support.

Nearly 8 in ten Germans say they are proud of supporting poorer countries. But only around 2 in ten say they understand what German development aid is actually trying to achieve.

In Argentina, young musicians show what that money can achieve. 

Skip next section Hamburg Pride returns with increased security a week after Berlin attack

Hamburg Pride returns with increased security a week after Berlin attack

Hundreds of thousands of people on Saturday gathered in the northern German port city of Hamburg for its annual Pride parade, one of Germany's biggest, one week after a deadly Islamist terrorist attack on Berlin Pride.

Among dozens of trucks marching through the center of Germany's second-biggest city was one representing Berlin's Pride event — known in Germany as Christopher Street Day or CSD for short.

Participants on the truck were asked to wear dark clothing in tribute to the victims of last week's attack.

"After the brutal attack on the CSD in Berlin, many are unsure in the queer community but also in society whether here and today is the right place," Hamburg's deputy mayor, Katharina Fegebank, told RTL television. "I say, now more than ever."

Both police and march organizers said the turnout was about 300,000 people.

Pride events also took place in Bonn and other cities across Germany.

Skip next section Rhine River hits record low in North Rhine-Westphalia

Rhine River hits record low in North Rhine-Westphalia

The river Rhine, one of the most important waterways in Germany, reached a historic low in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia on Saturday, authorities said.

Just 68 cm (26.77 inches) were measured at the gauge point in the city of Cologne, one centimeter below the previous record low of October 23, 2018.

The mean level at the gauge point ranges from 297 cm to 348 cm.

Gauge readings do not give the river's actual depth but rather the height of water above a given baseline. The shipping industry uses them to calculate what weights vessels using the waterway can carry.

The sinking water level comes as Germany, along with other parts of Europe, experiences low rainfall coupled with bouts of high summer temperatures that scientists say are a result of human-induced climate change.

The Rhine ⁠is an important ​route for commercial shipping and is used to transport commodities such as grains, minerals, ores, coal and oil products.

 A drought in 2022 that reduced water levels in the river caused supply bottlenecks and production problems affecting several companies.

Skip next section Forest fire breaks out in Bavaria

Forest fire breaks out in Bavaria

Some 330 emergency personnel have been deployed to fight a forest fire that broke out on Friday near Freudenberg in the Upper Palatinate region of Bavaria.

The fire is burning out of control in difficult terrain amid strong winds, local authorities said, with a thunderstorm hampering firefighting operations.

Four firefighters have been injured while battling the flames, local authorities said on Saturday.

People have been warned to avoid the area, while authorities have advised residents to keep windows and doors closed, turn off air conditioning and ventilation systems and follow local radio for further information.

Europe as a whole has seen several major blazes so far this seasonas human-induced climate change increasingly produces conditions conducive to their ignition.

Skip next section Train punctuality still 'not good' in first half of 2026 — DB head

Train punctuality still 'not good' in first half of 2026 — DB head

Just 58.7% of Germany's long-distance trains arrived on time at their destination in the first half of the year, with the head of national rail operator Deutsche Bahn (DB) conceding that there was much room for improvement.

"That is not a good figure. There's no point trying to gloss over it," Evelyn Palla told the Sunday edition of the Welt newspaper.

However, Palla, who took over as head of DB in October 2025, said the delay was less than 15 minutes in three-quarters of the cases.

"Even though we are not yet satisfied overall, we should not make Deutsche Bahn out to be worse than it is," she said.

DB considers a long-distance train delayed if it arrives at least six minutes late, with canceled trains included in the company's operational punctuality statistics.

Palla had set a punctuality target of at least 60% for this year and has worked to streamline the company by cutting several management positions, among other things.

DB has also begun to overhaul key lines as it seeks to improve its services, which have long been the object of criticism from those who rely on them. 

Skip next section Storms leave 1 dead in Saxony, cause disruption in Hamburg

Storms leave 1 dead in Saxony, cause disruption in Hamburg

A severe storm has hit the Saxon Switzerland region in the eastern state of Saxony, with a 28-year-old man killed by a falling tree, police said on Friday.

A number of other people were also injured, some seriously, amid the bad weather, they said.

The fatality occurred near the Felsenbühne open-air theater in the town of Rathen on Friday evening.

A performance of the musical "Little Shop of Horrors" at the theater, one of the largest open-air theaters in Saxony, was cancelled.

Parts of the Saxon Switzerland national park was closed to visitors on Saturday, with authorities saying there was still a risk from falling trees.

Germany's national meteorological service, the DWD, had issued warnings about severe thunderstorms for large parts of Saxony, saying there could be possible lightning strikes, falling trees and flying debris.

Meanwhile, a severe storm also swept the northern port city of Hamburg on Friday evening, with the fire brigade responding to almost 100 call-outs.

Most were water-related incidents.

No injuries were reported amid the storm, which was reported to have particularly affected the southern and northern outskirts of the city.

Skip next section Traffic disruption expected as Austrian pass road blocked

Traffic disruption expected as Austrian pass road blocked

Austria's Fern Pass road is to be closed for some two hours on Saturday morning amid a demonstration, with authorities warning of delays to holiday traffic as vacations get underway in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

The road is a key north-south transit route linking Germany, Austria and Italy.

Protesters are demonstrating not only at the volume of traffic on the route but also against a planned tunnel intended to replace the most difficult section of the road.

They say the project will only attract more traffic.

The nearby Hahntennjoch Pass will also be temporarily closed amid the protest, which is expected to be attended by hundreds of people.

The Fern Pass, which reaches an elevation of 1,212 meters (almost 4,000 feet), carries more traffic than almost any other pass in the eastern Alps, second only to the Brenner Pass.

entries.title: Moscow restaurant blast a 'brutal terror attack,' mayor says
entries.summary: The deadly explosion outside an upscale Moscow restaurant at Kudrinskaya Square was a "brutal terror attack," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, promising the perpetrators would be punished. But many questions remain.
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

The deadly explosion outside an upscale Moscow restaurant at Kudrinskaya Square was a "brutal terror attack," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, promising the perpetrators would be punished. But many questions remain.

An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described it as a "brutal terrorist attack."

"Law enforcement agencies are investigating the circumstances of the incident. Those responsible for this crime will certainly be found and face the punishment they deserve," he said in an online post on Sunday.

Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying  "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard.

The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron.

What do we know about the explosion?

State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC).

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event.

Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation.

Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack.

Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv. Russian officials have yet to comment on any possible Ukrainian involvement into the Kudrinskaya Square blast.

Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia overnight

However, Ukraine used drones to attack other parts of Russia on Saturday evening and early on Sunday, including a bombing which targeted an apartment block and killed two in the city Engels, some 900 kilometers (560 miles) southeast of Moscow.

Russia's Defense Ministry also said Kyiv struck a warehouse belonging to Wildberries, a major online retailer in Russia, with the Ukrainian drones hitting a site in the Samara Oblast, deep inside Russian territory. Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties.

Russian officials also reported over a 100 Ukrainian strikes in the Belgorod Oblast, which borders Ukraine. They said Kyiv forces used artillery, rocket launchers, and drones, leaving 14 people injured.

Over 200 Ukrainian drones have allegedly been shot down during the wave of attacks.

Overall, Russia claimed 635 downed Ukrainian drones overnight.

Meanwhile, at least one person was killed and seven wounded in the Russian attack on Ukraine's Kherson, with the attack involving artillery fire.

In Dnipro, seven passengers were wounded in a drone strike on a minibus, with the regional military administrator Oleksandr Hanzha describing it as a "deliberate and cynical attack on civilians."

At least nine people were killed and 33 injured in Russian strikes on Kyiv earlier this weekend.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Indonesia: At least 5 dead in ferry fire
entries.summary: Search and rescue officials report some 41 missing after a fire on a ferry near the Indonesia island of Madura. The cause of the blaze remains unclear.
entries.content:
Indonesia

Indonesia: At least 5 dead in ferry fire

August 2, 2026

Search and rescue officials report some 41 missing after a fire on a ferry near the Indonesia island of Madura. The cause of the blaze remains unclear.

At least five people have died and another 41 are missing after a ferry caught fire in Indonesia on Sunday morning, authorities have confirmed.

The Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferrywas carrying a total of 271 passengers and crew members from Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, across the Java Sea to Makassar in South Sulawesi.

Search and rescue officials said 225 people had been rescued by Sunday afternoon but that an operation was still ongoing.

Some passengers reportedly jumped overboard and were picked up by a nearby ship. Four other vessels were on standby nearby but could not approach because of the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, officials said.

What have Indonesian authorities said?

"Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site," said Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Indonesian Ministry of Transportation.

"The safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively," he added.

The fire, the cause of which remains unclear, was reported by the ship's captain who, according to officials, has not been in contact since.

Are shipping accidents common in Indonesia?

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where marine accidents are a regular occurrence, due to a combination of unpredictable weather conditions and lax safety standards.

Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small tropical island south of the much larger Sulawesi.

At least four people were found dead, and 14 others remained missing until the end of the search operation.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Poland: Prime Minister Tusk defies anti-Ukrainian violence
entries.summary: Anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland is on the rise, with numerous attacks against refugees from the war in Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has spoken out against the violence and warned of the danger from Russia.
entries.content:
Europe

Poland: Prime Minister Tusk defies anti-Ukrainian violence

August 2, 2026

Anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland is on the rise, with numerous attacks against refugees from the war in Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has spoken out against the violence and warned of the danger from Russia.

The Polish leader didn't mince his words. "We must wage a resolute fight against this violence, because thugs, hooligans, and this culture of violence are becoming increasingly brazen and insolent — and also because they have received political support," Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, before a Polish cabinet meeting in Warsaw. The liberal-conservative prime minister said he deplored the fact that "more and more such incidents" are taking place all over Poland.

Tusk's comments came in response to an incident in Wroclaw two days earlier, in which three Polish men brutally beat up a young Ukrainian man and his girlfriend on the street. Cellphone videos show the attackers kicking the Ukrainian man as he lies on the ground. The woman was also hit, sustaining injuries to her neck and ear.

The attack came after an argument in a shop; the attackers took exception to the couple's Ukrainian accents. Polish police acted swiftly: Two of the attackers, both of whom have previous convictions, are already in custody, and a third is being sought.

Tusk warned that such incidents negatively impact Poland's image abroad. The country's reputation was greatly enhanced by its willingness to provide assistanceafter the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. This could be destroyed, said Tusk, "if we allow thugs, hooligans and common criminals to beat and humiliate people just because they have a slightly different accent."

Mood is turning against Ukrainians

Poland provided military and humanitarian assistance to its neighbor from the very beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It took in more than one million refugees from the war, and around 1.5 million Ukrainians are currently living in Poland. The majority of them work, pay taxes, and contribute to the Polish economy.

But four and a half years after the start of the war, the mood in Poland has changed. More and more often, Ukrainians are being verbally and physically attacked in public. Last Wednesday a Polish manager on a construction site in Skawina, near Krakow, was filmed aggressively insulting Ukrainian workers. In another incident on a local train near Warsaw, two drunken men shouted verbal abuse at a Ukrainian passenger. On July 11, a man on a bus in Bielsko-Biala insulted and threatened two Ukrainian girls who were trying to take a selfie. Even schoolchildren, including teenagers at a playground, have fallen victim to the new climate of hate.

According to the police, 180 hate crimes against Ukrainians were recorded in the first six months of this year — a third more than in 2025. And on Friday (31.07.2026) the newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza warned that the internet is full of fake news about crimes Ukrainians are supposed to have committed against Poles.

Award of honorary title considered a provocation

Anti-Ukrainian slogans were already apparent during the presidential election campaign last year. But this May was a big turning point. The Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy prompted outrage in Poland with his decision to award a special unit of the Ukrainian army the honorary title of "Heroes of the UPA."

Poland holds the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) responsible for the mass murder of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia between 1943 and 1945. Ukrainians, on the other hand, revere the soldiers of the UPA as heroes in the fight against the Sovietization of their country. Individual UPA units continued to fight against Soviet rule well into the 1950s.

Along with Polish opposition politicians, Tusk is also critical of Zelenskyy in the row about the UPA. However, he believes that the reactions on both sides are exaggerated and counterproductive. Poland's president Karol Nawrocki revoked the award of Poland's highest order to his Ukrainian counterpart, which had been made in 2023. Zelenskyy returned the award by courier to Warsaw.

Avalanche of hate

These demonstrative gestures by both leaders have set off an avalanche. The Polish internet is flooded with hatred for Ukraine. Przemyslaw Czarnek, the prime ministerial candidate of the leading opposition Law and Justice party (PiS), demanded that all military aid for Ukraine be stopped until Kyiv backs down in the row over the interpretation of history.

Current opinion polls speak for themselves. According to a survey by the CBOS institute, for the first time since the start of the war a majority of respondents (54%) were opposed to taking in more Ukrainian refugees. Only 42% supported maintaining the policy to date. In 2022, at the start of the war, 94% of Poles wanted to offer sanctuary to refugees.

Another poll, by the Opinia24 institute for the weekly newspaper Polityka, found that 44% were against providing further aid to Ukraine, and 41% in favor. 54% of respondents opposed Ukraine joining the EU. Only 33% supported Kyiv's desire to become part of the European Union.

The Ukrainians who were attacked in Wroclaw spoke to the NEXTA Polska news service and urged their fellow countrymen to be careful while in Poland. They advised them to avoid any kind of conflict and to "speak less Ukrainian" in public, as a precaution.

Tusk wants to de-escalate the row with Ukraine

Poland's center-left government under prime minister Donald Tusk has emphatically condemned the anti-Ukrainian attacks. The Polish police and judiciary have also acted swiftly and decisively. After the incident in Wroclaw, Tusk urged President Nawrocki to "break his silence" and condemn the violence. So far, Poland's head of state still has not commented. During the presidential election campaign, Nawrocki, a former boxer, admitted that in his youth he took part in an organized brawl between fans of rival football clubs, violence he described as a form of "noble, masculine combat."

Tusk agrees with the opposition's criticism in the row about the UPA. All the same, he is trying to pour oil on troubled waters. On Wednesday, he met with the Ukrainian president Zelenskyy in private for the first time since the UPA crisis. "We also talked about the security challenges that, unfortunately, affect our people as well: it is important that Ukrainians who have left their homes because of the war and found refuge in Poland feel safe," Zelenskyy wrote afterwards on social media, and thanked Tusk.

Continued support for Ukraine

Polish-Ukrainian cooperation is vital for both countries, as demonstrated by an incident in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday (30.07.2026). During a massive Russian attack on Ukraine, a Russian rocket crossed into Polish airspace, landing in a field near a village around 90 kilometers inside the Polish border. The explosion left a crater ten meters wide.

"I know it's not very popular these days to speak well of Ukraine," Tusk said after visiting the scene. Nonetheless, the Polish leader continued: "Poland's security directly depends on the effective actions of Ukrainian forces, including in the air." Tusk stated: "I know where the enemy stands," and added that, despite protests by the Polish opposition, he remains committed to supplying weapons to Ukraine.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Germany: Islamism and right-wing extremism — a story of mutual radicalization
entries.summary: Following the attack on a Berlin Pride festival, the focus in Germany is turning to Islamist terrorism. An expert warns: Looking only at Islamists overlooks the parallels with right-wing extremism.
entries.content:
Germany

What unites Islamists and right-wing extremists

August 2, 2026

Following the attack on a Berlin Pride festival, the focus in Germany is turning to Islamist terrorism. An expert warns: Looking only at Islamists overlooks the parallels with right-wing extremism.

The terror attack on Berlin's Pride parade has shocked Germany. The perpetrator, 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, was a German national and known to German security forces as an Islamist who had tried to join the "Islamic State" group. He had already been convicted of criminal offences twice, and was awaiting a decision about a possible prison sentence at the time of the attack.

The LGBTQ+ community is not a surprising target, according to Jakob Guhl, a director of policy and research at the London-basedInstitute for Strategic Dialoguewho has studied Islamist extremism for many years. "The ideology is deeply homophobic and hostile to the queer community. The 'Islamic State' terror group, when it held territory in its so-called caliphate, executed people it accused of homosexuality," Guhl told DW.

In recent years, there have been several attacks on Pride events, Guhl said: In London, Oslo, Zurich and Vienna.

Parallels between different extremist movements

Guhl has also noticed that Islamist extremism has a close relationship with far-right extremist movements. Both ideologies strengthen each other and profit from one another, he argues: "Both are of the view that peaceful coexistence between Muslims and non-Muslims is impossible."

Young Muslims' experiences of discrimination in Germany, being marginalized, and negative reporting about Islam are cited as proof of the German state's hostility towards Islam, according to Guhl.

"In the view of the Islamist extremists, right-wing extremists are representative of Germans as a whole, and on the other hand the right-wing extremists say that Islamist extremists essentially represent Muslims," Guhl says. "There is an attempt to split society into two camps."

Both ideologies overlap in numerous attitudes: contempt for Western liberal society, the propensity toward conspiracy ideas, mistrust of government institutions, anti-feminist attitudes, and hate of the LGBTQ+ community.

"Their reasons for disliking the LGBTQ+ community do vary. On the one hand, from the religious ideological perspective, they believe it goes against the instructions of God," Guhl explained. "On the far-right extremist side, it mostly stems from a biological-racist perspective that it lowers the birthrate and weakens the health of the nation."

In Germany, security authorities have for years observed the formation of a new generation of young, violence-prone, far-right extremists who are mobilizing against Pride parades.

In a 2018 study entitled, "Loving hate. Anti-Muslim extremism, radical Islam and the spiral of polarization," Guhl and other authors described the common interest of both ideologies: Social division, itself a breeding ground for extremism.

Fuel for extremism: Hate speech on social media

To combat the proliferation of such ideologies, the authors recommended a tougher approach toward hate speech on social media. They also call upon traditional media to avoid one-sided reporting and finger-pointing, which only fuels the polarization spiral.

According to Guhl, one example of this is the current discussion about the background of the attacker of the Berlin Pride event. "I find the question of the nationality of the perpetrator problematic: You quickly run into the danger of creating a two-tier society between different affiliations. That is counterproductive when it comes to the dynamics of radicalization."

For Guhl, it is also important to keep pointing to what Muslim and non-Muslim communities have in common: "We share many more things than those which divide us."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Germany: As temperatures rise, so does climate skepticism
entries.summary: Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?

Climate skeptics are no longer a small but noisy minority. They are now "a mass phenomenon," according to researchers at Flensburg University.

In a study published in the scientific journal Global Environmental Change, authors Katharina Gies and Emanuel Deutschmann reported that between 2022 and 2023 there was a big jump in skeptical attitudes to climate change among the majority of the 3,074 people surveyed. Some 59% said they had more doubts about climate change in 2023 than they had had in the previous year.

The researchers wrote that the respondents' individual economic situations could not be considered the primary explanation for the increase in skepticism. Other factors, they said, were much more decisive: A right-leaning political orientation, distrust of state institutions, and dissatisfaction with democracy.

Social psychologist Marlene Altenmüller said the Flensburg publication is important and fascinating, though she has doubts about its alarming tone. Other studies show that "the number of people who have doubts is still very small," she says. Altenmüller, a junior professor at the Leibniz Institute for Psychology in Trier, conducts research into science reception: How people perceive scientific evidence, and what they think about the scientific system and its researchers.

Altenmüller's research indicates that people in Germany do not have fundamental doubts about scientific evidence. Rather, it varies depending on the topic, and the view the group to which people feel they belong has of the topic.

If a group has doubts about climate change, so do its members

Her work, and that of many other researchers, also shows that politically right-leaning people express more skepticism about climate change.

"If right-wing parties were suddenly to discover that we should in fact take action against climate change, my assumption is that the followers of these parties would also believe in climate change and would support political measures," Altenmüller said.

Nor does she believe that climate skeptics have a different personality structure. Instead, climate skepticism is more likely to be down to the fact that "people orientate themselves according to their group and its identity." The credo for most people is that content is secondary, or, as Altenmüller calls it, "Party over policy."

Underlying this is something psychologists call motivated reception. People always see the world through the lens of their own desires, ideas, values, and political ideologies, and anything that cannot be squared with their own ideas and values tends to be disparaged. Altenmüller's research demonstrates that all of us are predisposed to seeing the world through our own filters.

From climate skepticism to conspiracy theories

Both Altenmüller and the Flensburg researchers emphasize that climate change skepticism comes in different guises. One form is the rejection of climate policy measures. The basis for this may be the assumption that it won't be all that bad, or doubt that human activity is the cause. Another is the belief that all the talk about climate change is simply a con, a conspiracy.

This is the focus of research of Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive science at the universities of Bristol and Potsdam. Among other things, he examines the persistence of misinformation and conspiracy theories, and is interested in the parameters that determine whether people reject or accept scientific proofs, especially in connection with vaccines and climate change. "Certain people are more susceptible to conspiracy theories than others," he said.

The COVID-19 pandemic made this very apparent. Lewandowsky argues that for some people, conspiracy theories that apportion blame for a particular situation provide a welcome opportunity to escape from feelings like fear and loss of control. "That offers some brief psychological comfort to people," Lewandowsky says.

However, he goes on to explain that the comfort they derive from assigning blame does not last long. "There's good evidence to suggest that people who do fall into that rabbit hole over time are suffering," he said. "They're less likely to hold their jobs. They lose social contacts. They become mentally challenged."

Why climate skepticism is hardly an issue in India

Climate skepticism and conspiracy theories are mostly a Western phenomenon. Researchers observe them the most in the US, Europe, and Australia. In India and other countries of the global south, climate change is already a question of daily survival, and has been for some time. "In India, a lot of people still suffer from [not] getting access to clean drinking water," says Jagadish Thaker, senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, Australia, and an expert in climate change communication.

For years now, he says, people in the global south have been experiencing first-hand the ways that climate change is exacerbating problems through rising temperatures and extreme weather events.

Consequently, measures to reduce emissions and adapt to changing living conditions are not seen as a matter of political ideology. According to Thaker, people in India are trying to counteract their own vulnerability to climate change while still trying to develop economically.

Countering climate skepticism with respect

Heatwaves and other extreme weather events are a direct threat to human life in Germany, as has become apparent during this summer's heatwaves, which are reported to have killed as many as 10,000 people already. 

This is why the authors of the Flensburg study are urging people to take climate change skepticism seriously if they are to successfully anchor climate protection measures in society.

Thaker believes the media plays a decisive role. He believes there is still a general lack of information and understanding of the effects of climate change. "The media coverage of extreme weather events, while it's a lot, it is dramatic, and unfortunately doesn't mention climate change."

Altenmüller says it's important to keep emphasizing that there is a scientific consensus that climate change is anthropogenic, or, caused by human activity. Sometimes, she says, it does matter who says it. Research shows that some scientific disciplines are perceived as more biased than others. Consequently, economists have a better chance of their message reaching a wide audience than sociologists.

Taking the values of people who express skepticism into account could also help to communicate a different point of view to them, says Altenmüller. Communication must emphasize not only the restrictions that need to be imposed through political measures, but also the opportunities arising from this.

People who have themselves experienced extreme weather events probably find it easier to shift their perspective. This is why Lewandowsky is hopeful that the this year's heatwaves and wildfires will make a difference. "At some point, people's personal experiences matter," he says.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: China: Dozens dead in Gansu flash floods
entries.summary: Chinese authorities will launch an investigation into the floods, amid warnings of further landslides as the rainy weather continues.
entries.content:
Asia

China: Dozens dead in Gansu flash floods

August 2, 2026

Chinese authorities will launch an investigation into the floods, amid warnings of further landslides as the rainy weather continues.

The death toll after a flash flood in the northern Gansu province of China has climbed to 25, according to state media reports.

The flood has left 23 others injured, the ⁠official Xinhua news agency reported on Sunday.

What do we know about the Gansu flash floods?

The Shuangshimen Scenic Area, a popular tourist spot for camping, was hit by a flash flood on July 26, with state media initially reporting 10 deaths and 23 injuries.

The country's national commission for disaster prevention said it would oversee an investigation into the event.

Videos of the flood show a deluge ripping through a valley where several tents and cars were parked.

Authorities have warned of further landslides, including in ‌Dingxi, ​as heavy downpour continues in the annual flood season.

Beijing and Inner Mongolia also issued weather warnings on Sunday as China's ​weather observatory warned of heavy rain, high winds and thunderstorms across a large stretch of the country from ⁠the southwest ​to the northeast.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: On the front line of Europe's battle against wildfires
entries.summary: French firefighters have won out over a massive blaze, with almost 200,000 evacuees returning home. But Europe's climate-fueled wildfire season is far from over.
entries.content:
August 2, 2026

French firefighters have won out over a massive blaze, with almost 200,000 evacuees returning home. But Europe's climate-fueled wildfire season is far from over.

The signal to move comes suddenly — and within a minute or so the fire truck is full and speeding off into the distance, a cloud of orange dust swirling in its wake. "There's always a bit of adrenaline when you get the call," marine firefighter Julien says. "But we're trained; we're prepared."

Maitre Julien — whom DW can only identity by rank and first name — is part of Marseille-based battalion deployed to France's Gironde region to tackle a wildfire which prompted the largest evacuations in the country since World War II.

Some 264 firefighters were injured in the fight against the Gironde fire, four of whom lost their lives. In nearby towns, French flags still fly at half mast to mark the loss. "It's always on our mind," Lieutenant Damien, another marine firefighter, explains as his team members haul the firehose out behind him.

Big battles on little sleep

Letitia, a firefighter and medic, said she tries to ask how colleagues are feeling "without being too intrusive."

"It's the fatigue above all," she says when asked about the most common problem affecting her colleagues. "They're sleeping very little."

"Do you see all all of that?" Maitre Julien asks, gesturing out the car window as he drives past rows of blackened trees and swathes of scorched earth at the roadside. "All of that's already burned. But you can see small peels of smoke here and there. We absolutely have to extinguish those so fires don't restart."

When Julien pulls up at another hotspot, the risk of flare-ups comes sharply into focus: The air smells burned and a cloud of white smoke fills the sky. Within about 20 minutes, the smoke turns thick and black, and the fire — previously under control — was visible burning bright again through the trees.

Here by the firefighters' side are improvised teams of local volunteers — farmers and tradesmen and women who took it upon themselves to use their tractors or vans or four-by-fours to transport water to firefighters on the front line, and often head into the blazes themselves without proper protective gear or training.

"We're here because we're needed. And because we want to help," Steven Page, one volunteer, told DW. Maitre Julien said they played a "primordial" role, saving firefighters "precious time" in the fight.

Winning a 'David and Goliath' fight, together

At times, firefighters said, this felt like a "David and Goliath" battle. But they came out on top. By Saturday, France's Interior Ministry declared the fire was no longer progressing. Most of the 220,000 evacuees were allowed to return home.

Elsewhere in Europe, the heat of battle is far from over: Wildfires have also been raging in Greece and Spain — other countries are likely to face fires in the coming months too.

That's keeping EU crisis management chief Hadja Lahbib busy. She visited Bordeaux on Thursday, meeting local officials in Ornano fire station's crisis room and learning how they felled trees and vegetation across 150 kilometers (93 miles) of land to create tactical firebreaks and prevent the flames from reaching the city.

Dotted around the green lines on the map representing firebreaks are different European flags: Germany, Slovakia, Portugal, Spain, Belgium, Sweden, Czechia, Switzerland, Turkey — some of the countries that sent firefighting aircraft, firefighting crews, and technical teams through the EU's crisis management mechanism.

More EU funds to fight climate-fueled fires?

"Climate change isn't knocking at our door. It's here," Lahbib told DW on Thursday. Last year, her team laid out an EU crisis preparedness plan designed to better anticipate and prevent wildfires and other disasters through EU cooperation. "For that we need the means," she said.

"We proposed a budget of €10.7 billion ($12.3 billion), which is an important amount of money, but at the same time, it pays back," she said. "It's better to prevent — to anticipate — then to recover. So I hope that member states will follow our proposal."

EU states pay into a communal seven-year budget for the bloc. Some national governments facing their own financial woes — including Germany — are skeptical about the EU Commission's bid to lock in its biggest-ever global budget.

Lessons for the future

Climate campaigners also accuse the EU of walking back on big green promises as the bloc pursues a red-tape-cutting agenda to better compete with the likes of China and the US.

"This isn't 'just nature.'⁣ Decades of burning coal, oil and gas are making wildfires more frequent and more destructive," Greenpeace wrote in a statement last week.

But ⁣Lahbib gave a cautious response when asked about allegations that EU states were dragging their feet on climate action. "This is not the moment for controversy and so on. This is a moment of solidarity," she said. "We will have the time to draw on the lessons learned."

In Brussels, where a small monitoring and decision team runs a bloc-wide crisis response center, unit chief Maria Zuber is already busy planning.

"We need to think of informing the population," she said. "We need to think of evacuation plans. We need to invest in early warning tools. So all this is something that we we are mapping. I think that is the main challenge — that we need to change our mindset."

Wildfire season far from over

Back in Gironde, Maitre Julien is all too aware of what's ahead. "We know we'll have more intense fires like this one more frequently," he said. Even this year's wildfire season isn't over yet — Julien and his team still have all of August and September to get through.

But for now, there's a moment of reprieve. At a hastily setup command center in Lège-Cap-Ferret, firefighters can get a meal and some rest before heading back home, or out on their next shift. There's little privacy — just rows of camp beds in a sports hall full of people. Outside, some firefighters prefer to lie on the ground in the shade of empty firetrucks.

"It's a little moment of cohesion," Maitre Julien explains as he sips coffee and jokes with volunteers. "We're not with our family, so we make this sort of temporary bubble to stay well. So that it's more like home."

Tessa Walther contributed to this article.

Edited by Ben Knight

entries.title: No new Iran strikes for now amid deal hopes — Trump
entries.summary: Donald Trump says the US and Israel have agreed to hold off on strikes on Iran if a peace deal is reached "rapidly." Iran has vowed a decisive response to any new aggression. DW has more.
entries.content:
Iran

No new Iran strikes for now amid deal hopes — Trump

Published August 1, 2026last updated August 2, 2026

Donald Trump says the US and Israel have agreed to hold off on strikes on Iran if a peace deal is reached "rapidly." Iran has vowed a decisive response to any new aggression. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • President Donald Trump says the US and Israel will refrain from threatened strikes on Iran to give diplomacy another chance
  • Trump nonetheless said that the US was 'locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran'
  • Iran has warned against any 'adventurous action' by the US

Read below for all the latest headlines on the Iran war on the weekend of August 1-2.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Israeli airstrikes kill several in Gaza despite ceasefire

Israeli airstrikes kill several in Gaza despite ceasefire

Israeli strikes have killed at least eight people in the Gaza Strip on a second consecutive day of aerial attacks.

The continued attacks come despite an announcement by US President Donald Trump that the Palestinian militant group Hamas had agreed to disarm under a US-backed initiative ​to implement a ceasefire agreement reached last year.

Palestinian health officials said Israeli warplanes carried out separate strikes ​across the enclave: In Gaza City in the north, the city of Deir al-Balah in the center, and in Khan Younis in the south.

Those killed included at least two children, medics said.

The Israeli military said the strikes in Deir al-Balah targeted two commanders of Hamas' ‌elite "Nukhba" ​force. It said strikes in Gaza City and nearby Jabalia also targeted "military operatives" but that it was still reviewing the situation.

Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,230 Palestinians since the ceasefire was reached in October.

Israel began an offensive against Hamas in the Gaza Strip after the group, designated as a terrorist organization by several countries, led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023, in which some 1,200 people were killed, the majority of them civilians.

More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in the conflict, a toll given by Palestinian authorities but one that the United Nations broadly accepts.

The figure does not differentiate between militants and civilians.

Skip next section Trump claim that Tehran requested attack stop 'a new lie,' Iran says

Trump claim that Tehran requested attack stop 'a new lie,' Iran says

US President Donald Trump's claim that Tehran had asked the US to hold off on new strikes was completely false, Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency said on Sunday. 

Citing military officials, the agency said the claim "was nothing but a new lie" and that Iran's military was "on high alert and ready for any eventuality."

Trump said on Saturday that the US and Israel had agreed to refrain from new attacks he had threatened after requests "by Iran, and other Middle Eastern countries."

Skip next section Israeli military says kills several Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon

Israeli military says kills several Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon

The Israeli military said that it has killed several Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon.

In a statement on Sunday, the Israeli military said it had identified several Hezbollah militants inside an area occupied by Israeli forces that Israel has designated as a "security zone." 

       

"Following the identification, the soldiers struck the terrorists and eliminated them in order to remove the threat," the military said in a statement.

An Israeli soldier sustained moderate injuries, the military said earlier.

Pro-Iran Hezbollah brought Lebanon into the wider Middle East conflict when it fired rockets at Israel on March 2 in reaction to the US, Israeli attacks on Iran.

That act triggered major Israeli airstrikes and a ground invasion, with Israel continuing military operations deep into the south of Lebanon since then.

Under a US-sponsored framework agreement signed by Lebanon and Israel in late June, Lebanon's army is to disarm Hezbollah and the Israeli military is to withdraw from "pilot zones" inside Lebanon to be replaced by Lebanese forces.

Hezbollah, however, refuses to disarm, and there has been no timetable set for Israel's full withdrawal.

Skip next section Saudi crown prince calls for dialogue and de-escalation in call with Trump

Saudi crown prince calls for dialogue and de-escalation in call with Trump

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman stressed "the necessity of prioritizing dialogue to de-escalate tensions" with Iran in a phone call with US President Donald Trump on Saturday, according to Saudi Arabia's state news agency.

Increased calm "would pave the way for diplomatic solutions [...] and prevent a slide into a broader conflict with repercussions affecting regional and international security and stability," the agency said, apparently citing bin Salman, the de facto ruler of Saudi Arabia.

The agency said that "the call also reviewed existing areas of cooperation between the two countries and ways to enhance them."

The report confirms similar accounts in US media about a telephone call between the two, which came shortly before Trump said he would hold off on fresh attacks on Iran that he had threatened.

Skip next section Iran warns against new US aggression

Iran warns against new US aggression

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday warned that Tehran's armed forces would respond decisively to any act of aggression.

His message on Telegram came after US President Trump made his since-rescinded threats of fresh strikes, and also followed a call with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan.

In the post, Araghchi said the US, Israel and any Gulf states involved would bear full responsibility for any new attacks.

Tehran had already threatened military retaliation targeting critical infrastructure in Israel and Gulf countries after US media reports that Washington was thinking about major new strikes on Iranian targets, including energy sites.

Since the war began on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic, Iran has already often responded to any strikes by targeting Gulf states hosting US military bases.

Skip next section Trump says no new strikes on Iran if peace deal is reached soon

Trump says no new strikes on Iran if peace deal is reached soon

US President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States and Israel had agreed to refrain from carrying out threatened attacks on Iran under the condition that a peace deal with Tehran was reached quickly.

Trump said the US was "locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran," but that Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked him not to carry out fresh strikes.

"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.

"The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE," he added.

His remarks come after he on Friday threatened to hit Iran "very hard," with reports saying US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure were being considered.

According to the US media reports, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke with Trump before Saturday's social media postings to express concerns over the reports of planned new attacks.

The report, which cited US sources close to the talks, said the crown prince urged Trump to de-escalate.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

We are resuming our reporting on events in the Middle East as the more-than-five-month-long US war on Iran continues to ebb and flow.

Sunday seems likely to see another at least temporary ebb, with US President Donald Trump — who on Friday threatened to hit Iran "very hard" — saying the US and Israel had agreed to hold off on new strikes on the Islamic Republic if a peace deal is "rapidly" reached.

Iran, meanwhile, has reacted to Friday's threat by saying its armed forces would give a decisive response to any renewed acts of aggression.

Read on for more details about the conflict in the Middle East, which is threatening to draw in ever more countries in the region.

Skip next section We've paused coverage

We've paused coverage

US President Donald Trump told reporters on Friday he expected US military action against Iran to continue for some time. He said the US will hit Iran "very hard" until they can't take it anymore.

Hours later on Saturday, Kuwait said it responded to a new round of drone attacks from Iran while a tanker was struck in the strategic waterway.

We'll have more on each of those major news angles when we return to this blog on Sunday.

Skip next section UN warns against ongoing destruction in southern Lebanon

UN warns against ongoing destruction in southern Lebanon

The United Nations on Saturday said it is deeply concerned by ongoing Israeli demolitions in southern Lebanon.

Under a ceasefire deal, Lebanon's army is expected to disarm Iran-backed Hezbollah, while Israeli forces withdraw from designated zones in the south before Lebanese troops deploy.

"The scale of the detonations and demolitions taking place in south Lebanon is deeply concerning, with a devastating impact on civilian infrastructure, cultural heritage, and the collective memory of communities," the office of the UN special coordinator for Lebanon said in a statement on X.

The statement comes a day after the Israeli military triggered explosions near Beaufort Castle in southern Lebanon, which was added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger last week.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army destroyed "terror tunnels in the Beaufort area" using around 700 tonnes of explosives.

"The escalating pattern of destruction must stop as diplomatic channels exist to resolve any outstanding issues," the UN said.

Skip next section Gaza authorities say three killed in Israeli attacks

Gaza authorities say three killed in Israeli attacks

Israeli airstrikes killed three people in the Gaza Strip on Saturday according to Palestinian civil defense and health authority sources.

Israel said it had targeted "terrorists" and dismantled five weapons storage facilities in Saturday operations.

The attacks came on the heels of a recent announcement by US President Donald Trump promising the Islamist militant group Hamas would disarm and Israel's army would withdraw from Gaza.

Hamas led the October 7, 2023, surprise attacks on Israel that sparked the war in Gaza.

According to sources in the enclave, two Palestinians were killed in drone strikes in Gaza City and another man was killed during a missile strike on a hospital camp in Deir al-Balah.

Footage of the camp showed a large crater and scattered medical equipment, medical supplies and boxes near tents and two warehouses.

Israel accused Hamas of establishing a weapons depot at the site, citing intelligence reports without making evidence public.

Hospital workers said the warehouses were used to store essential dialysis equipment and supplies and that many people in need of critical medical care had been sheltering in tents near the site. 

A ceasefire has been in place in Gaza since October 2025, but Israel has recently killed suspected members of Hamas and the Islamic Jihad militant group there.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not commented on Trump's ceasefire plan for Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and Hamas disarmament. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has called the deal unacceptable, demanding the continuation of Israeli military operations in Gaza.

Skip next section Israel claims to have killed several Hezbollah fighters

Israel claims to have killed several Hezbollah fighters

Israel's military on Saturday said its forces killed several Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon. A post on the military's official X account said that one of its combat officers was injured during the armed encounter and had been hospitalized.

The post pledged that the Israeli military would "continue to operate to remove any threat its forces and will not allow the Hezbollah terror organization to harm the citizens of the state of Israel."

The incident came despite a ceasefire being in place between Israel and the Iranian-backed militants. While Hezbollah has formally denounced the deal, the group has not claimed any attacks since theUS-sponsored framework agreement was signed by Israel and Lebanon and then put in place in late June.

The agreement remains fragile, with Hezbollah refusing to disarm and Israel refusing to leave southern Lebanon — both points outlined in the agreement.

Despite the relative decline in violence in southern Lebanon, Israel has continued to conduct airstrikes and carry out other military operations.

Lebanon has condemned Israel's operations, saying that its continued military operations make it impossible to fully deploy the Lebanese army as outlined in the deal.

Skip next section US urges citizens to prepare to leave Middle East

US urges citizens to prepare to leave Middle East

US embassies across the Middle East have urged US nationals to consider leaving the region or be ready to depart if the conflict escalates further.

"Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation," security alerts posted by US missions in Amman, Jerusalem and Baghdad said.

The warnings told citizens to check flight information, follow local safety instructions and prepare for cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruption.

Those in Jordan were advised to stay away from US military bases, which have recently come under Iranian missile attack.

In Israel, US citizens were urged to identify the nearest bomb shelter.

"The Iranian regime is unpredictable," the US Embassy in Jerusalem said, citing recent attacks across the region and an expansion to areas not previously targeted, including Egypt.

A drone struck a US-owned gas vessel moored at an Egyptian port on Wednesday, sparking a fire. Egyptian authorities are investigating and have not publicly blamed any group.

Skip next section New attacks hit Kuwait and Strait of Hormuz shipping

New attacks hit Kuwait and Strait of Hormuz shipping

Kuwait's military says it is responding to a fresh wave of Iranian drone attacks that struck several "vital facilities" in the country.

Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi said the targets included a government facility in northern Kuwait. No casualties were reported.

Separate incidents also hit commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said an unidentified projectile struck a tanker on Friday about 11 nautical miles (20 kilometers) northeast of Lima, Oman, damaging its engine room.

On Saturday, another tanker reported a large splash and an explosion nearby while sailing around 21 nautical miles northwest of Khasab.

No casualties were reported in either maritime incident.

Iran has repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its authorization during the conflict with the United States.

Skip next section Houthis claim Saudi oil shipments diverted

Houthis claim Saudi oil shipments diverted

Yemen's Houthi movement says eight Saudi oil tankers have been pushed off their usual routes as part of a newly declared blockade targeting the kingdom's energy exports.

According to the Iran-backed group, the ships will now have to make the much longer journey around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope to reach Asian markets.

Riyadh has not confirmed that any tankers were diverted.

The Houthis announced the blockade last week, framing it as retaliation for what they describe as years of Saudi pressure on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

The group controls much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, after seizing territory in 2014 and setting off a war that drew in a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognized government.

A major concern for global shipping is the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow passage between Yemen and the Horn of Africa that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Any serious disruption there would add to pressure on trade routes already affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis said they do not intend to levy transit charges on vessels using the strait.

Skip next section Iran warns regional states against helping US

Iran warns regional states against helping US

Iran's military has accused the United States of "escalating tensions" in the Middle East and warned regional neighbors against supporting Washington during the conflict.

"The United States is rapidly moving down the path of escalating tensions in the region," Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran's military central command, said in a statement broadcast on state television on Saturday.

"Any country serving as [a] defensive shield for criminal and aggressive America will be engulfed by the flames of war," he added.

The warning came after US President Donald Trump again threatened to hit Iran "very hard."

US media reported that Trump was considering renewed large-scale strikes as early as this weekend, potentially including attacks on energy infrastructure.

Iran and the United States resumed exchanges of fire this week after several days of relative calm, although no strikes were reported overnight from Friday into Saturday.

entries.title: US: Multiple dead in shooting at In-N-Out Burger in Idaho
entries.summary: Multiple people were killed in a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in southern Idaho. The suspected shooter is dead, police said.
entries.content:
North America

US: Multiple dead in shooting at In-N-Out Burger in Idaho

August 2, 2026

Multiple people were killed in a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in southern Idaho. The suspected shooter is dead, police said.

Multiple people were killed and others were injured after a gunman opened fire at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in a city in the northwestern US state of Idaho.

The shooting unfolded near a busy shopping area in Twin Falls where hundreds of people were present, police chief Matthew Hicks said in a news conference.

The suspected shooter was among the dead, Hicks said. Police were still trying to determine the shooter's identity and motive.

Local media broadcast video footage from the scene showing what appeared to be a young man carrying a long gun outside the restaurant that had only been open for a week at the Twin Falls location.

Police to confirm exact number of fatalities

The shooting at the burger chain "resulted in fatalities" but authorities were still working to determine the number of victims, Hicks said.

"We are working to try to ascertain his identity and the motivations behind [the shooting] and we'll be able to figure that out in the next coming days," he said, adding that it was a "very chaotic scene."

Local public radio station KTVB reported that three people were killed and two were injured. A city spokesperson said the number of victims is expected to be higher.

Multiple people hospitalized after shooting at Idaho In-N-Out

Police said multiple people were taken to St. Luke's Magic Valley Medical Center.

Hospital spokesperson Taylor Marschner said in a statement that it was "working closely with law enforcement and emergency responders as they manage the situation."

Twin Falls, a city of about 56,000 people, is about 130 miles (205 kilometers) southeast of Boise and about 75 miles (120 kilometers) north of the Nevada border.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar
